findings.title: Transpose full writes a sparse array, poisoning lower tracks
findings.whats_wrong: Dragging 'Transpose full' on any track other than the first corrupts every track above it. The code assigns into a hole of an empty array, and AlphaTab then reads the holes back as NaN for the lower-indexed staves - garbage drawn pitches, and a silent channel on the next MIDI rebuild.
findings.proposed_fix: In setTrackTransposition, densify before writing: `const pitches = [...api.settings.notation.transpositionPitches]; while (pitches.length <= trackIndex) pitches.push(0); pitches[trackIndex] = semitones;` - 0 is AlphaTab's own "no transposition" value and is what toMixerTrack already reports for every untouched row.
findings.why_it_works: Filling the gap with 0 - AlphaTab's own 'no transposition' value, and what the mixer already reports for untouched rows - means the loop reads a real number for every index instead of undefined. It fixes the lower tracks without changing what the dragged track does.
findings.why_it_matters: Dragging "Transpose full" on any track other than the first breaks every track ABOVE it in the score. `pitches[trackIndex] = semitones` on an array that is still `[]` (AlphaTab ships `transpositionPitches = []`, and `clearTrackTranspositions` resets it to `[]` on every file open) produces a sparse array with holes at indexes 0..trackIndex-1. AlphaTab's `applyPitchOffsets` then runs `staff.transpositionPitch = -settings.notation.transpositionPitches[i]` for every `i < length`, so a hole becomes `-undefined` = `NaN`: on a melodic track that makes `Note.calculateRealValue` return NaN, and the staff redraws with garbage pitches and "NaN" fret numbers. The same holes reach the synth on the next MIDI rebuild — `MidiFileGenerator._generateChannel` reads `settings.notation.transpositionPitches[track.index]`, gets `undefined`, and `channelNoteOn` does `key += undefined`, so that channel goes silent. Padding the array with zeros up to `trackIndex` before the write removes the holes and matches what AlphaTab expects (a dense per-track array).

findings.title: Setting is persisted before the engine is asked to accept it
findings.whats_wrong: An edit is written to localStorage BEFORE the engine is asked to accept it, and the live apply has no try/catch. So a value AlphaTab rejects is already stored; on every later visit the restore hits the same rejection and throws away the entire saved settings document.
findings.proposed_fix: Reorder `applySetting` to apply-then-persist under a guard: wrap `if (api) applySettingsJson(api, next, apply);` in `try { ... } catch { setSettings(settings); toast.error('That value could not be applied.'); return; }` and move `localStorage.setItem(...)` below it so it runs only on success.
findings.why_it_works: The engine becomes the gate. Nothing reaches storage that the engine has not already accepted, so the permanent-restore-break in #11 stops being reachable at all, and the person sees an error at the moment of the edit instead of silently losing every setting later.
findings.why_it_matters: Any value AlphaTab rejects outlives the failure: the edit funnel writes the new settings document to localStorage first and only then hands it to the engine, and unlike the engine-build call at PlayerShell.tsx:241-245 the live `applySettingsJson` carries no try/catch. So when `fillFromJson` throws (an unparseable font today -- see the font-row finding -- and any future row whose parser is strict), the person sees an uncaught error, the engine is left half-updated, and the value that caused it is already stored and comes back on every reload. Applying first inside a try/catch and persisting only on success makes the store reflect what the engine actually accepted, and matches the guard the engine-build path already uses.
evidence: web/app/play/PlayerShell.tsx:568 -- `        globalThis.localStorage.setItem(SETTINGS_STORAGE_KEY, serializeSettings(next));`  -- runs before the engine has seen the value
web/app/play/PlayerShell.tsx:573 -- `      if (api) applySettingsJson(api, next, apply);`  -- no try/catch here, unlike the engine-build call
web/lib/alphatab/live-settings.ts:59 -- `  api.settings.fillFromJson(json as AlphaTab.json.SettingsJson);`  -- the throwing call, unguarded on this path
web/app/play/PlayerShell.tsx:241-245 -- the parallel pattern this path should match: `try { engineSettings.fillFromJson(settings as AlphaTab.json.SettingsJson); } catch { ... }`
findings.verifier_reason: The storage write at :568 precedes applySettingsJson at :573, and that call has no try/catch. fillFromJson routes elementFonts through Font.fromJson, whose FontParser throws on a malformed string. So a rejected value is already in storage, loadStoredSettings keeps it (same type), and the init-time fillFromJson then discards EVERY stored setting on each later visit.

findings.title: Font rows ship without the validator their row contract requires
findings.whats_wrong: All twelve font rows accept any string. SettingRow only validates a text row when the row supplies a validator, and none of them do. Clear a font field and press Enter and AlphaTab's font parser throws - after the bad value has already been persisted (see #5), so the player stops restoring settings from then on.
findings.proposed_fix: Add one shared validator in settings-schema.ts and pass it on all twelve `kind: 'text'` rows, e.g. `const validateFont = (draft: string) => /^(?:(?:normal|italic|oblique|small-caps|bold|bolder|lighter|[1-9]00)\s+)*\d+(?:\.\d+)?(?:px|pt|em|rem)\s+\S/.test(draft.trim());` then `control: { kind: 'text', validate: validateFont }`. Assumption: the accepted shape is the CSS font shorthand the shipped defaults already use.
findings.why_it_works: A validator is the mechanism SettingRow already provides for exactly this; the rows simply never used it. Rejecting a malformed string at the field stops it reaching both the engine and storage, so it closes the input half of the same failure #5 closes on the ordering half.
findings.why_it_matters: Clear a font field in the Settings popover and press Enter (or type 'bold') and the player stops restoring settings correctly from then on, silently and permanently. SettingRow only gates a text row on `control.validate`, and none of the twelve `kind: 'text'` font rows supply one, so the raw string is reported, written to localStorage, and handed to `Settings.fillFromJson`, where AlphaTab's `FontParser` throws (`_fontSizeLineHeight` -> `throw new Error('Missing font size')`, alphaTab.core.mjs:27319). The bad string is now stored; every later visit re-throws inside the engine-build `fillFromJson`, which is caught at PlayerShell.tsx:243, so the restore is truncated at that key and every setting after it is silently never applied. `loadStoredSettings` type-checks a string against a string default and returns `reset: false`, so no toast fires and no repair write happens -- the person's only way out is to find that exact row again or clear site data. Supplying the `validate` the component already accepts (as SettingRow.tsx:47 and :163 say the caller must) keeps the unparseable draft from ever reaching storage or the engine.

findings.title: Unguarded localStorage read leaves the player page permanently broken
findings.whats_wrong: The player page reads localStorage inside a useState initialiser, guarded only against server-side rendering. In a browser that blocks site data the getter itself throws, during render, so the whole /play page falls over to its error boundary. Both localStorage WRITES in the same file are wrapped in try/catch; only the read is not.

findings.proposed_fix: Wrap the read in the lazy initialiser: `try { return loadStoredSettings(globalThis.localStorage.getItem(SETTINGS_STORAGE_KEY), DEFAULT_PLAYER_SETTINGS, SETTING_OPTION_VALUES); } catch { return { settings: DEFAULT_PLAYER_SETTINGS, reset: false }; }`. findings.why_it_works: It makes the read match the writes the same file already guards. Blocked storage is a different condition from a corrupt document, so returning reset:false keeps the toast and the repair write out of it - the person just gets shipped defaults and a working player.
findings.why_it_matters: In a browser configured to block site data (Chrome's 'block all cookies', Firefox with dom.storage disabled, a partitioned third-party context), touching `globalThis.localStorage` throws a SecurityError. findings.title: Open file/drop is a silent no-op after a dismissed engine-import failure
findings.whats_wrong: After AlphaTab's module import fails once, the failure is cached for the whole page. The error banner is dismissible for the first time in this PR - and once dismissed, 'Open file' and drag-and-drop do nothing at all: no toast, no error, nothing. The code's own comment claims Open file 'is the actual way back', which is false in that state.
findings.proposed_fix: In requestNotation (PlayerShell.tsx:646-653), replace the bare `if (!at) return;` with a branch that also calls toast.error('The player could not start, so this file cannot be opened. Reload the page and try again.', { id: 'notation-load' }) before returning, mirroring the toast.error(..., { id: 'notation-load' }) call used later in the same function for a file that fails to parse.
findings.why_it_works: It reuses the toast id the same function already uses for a file that fails to parse, so the two failure paths behave alike and the person learns why nothing happened. It does not try to revive the engine - that stays a reload, which the message now says.
findings.why_it_matters: When AlphaTab's self-hosted ESM import fails (a CDN blip, a blocked script, a stale cached chunk), the header shows a banner this PR makes dismissible for the first time (`web/app/play/NotationSurface.tsx:90,220-224`, all newly added lines). Once the person dismisses it -- the button's only function -- the code's own comment says 'Open file' in the left rail is 'the actual way back', but `requestNotation` retries the SAME memoised `loadAlphaTabEngine()` promise, which `web/lib/alphatab/engine.ts:33-37` documents as permanently cached as a rejection ('one failed import is permanent for the page ... the `.catch(() => null)` retry ... cannot succeed after a failure'). The retry resolves to `null` and the function returns at line 652 with no toast, no state change, and no loading indicator -- the click (or a file drop) does visibly nothing. Both entry points are affected the same way: `OpenFileControl.tsx:64-75` and the drop-zone's `acceptDropped` each await `requestNotation` inside their own try/catch, but since it resolves normally rather than throwing, neither catch ever fires. Before this PR the banner could not be dismissed, so the failure was always visible; now the one indicator can be hidden while the one advertised recovery path fails in total silence, leaving the person with no way to learn a reload is required. Adding a `toast.error(..., { id: 'notation-load' })` at the `if (!at) return;` branch -- the same pattern `requestNotation` already uses a few lines later for a file that fails to parse, and that `OpenFileControl`/`acceptDropped` already use for their own failures -- closes the gap for both entry points at once.

findings.title: Settings popover rebuilds all 90 rows on every keystroke (unmemoized)
findings.whats_wrong: The 90-row settings schema is rebuilt on every render of the popover's parent, which re-renders about once per animation frame while the transport is running - so the whole descriptor tree is reconstructed roughly 60 times a second whether or not the popover is even open.
findings.proposed_fix: Memoize the schema build: const groups = useMemo(() => (engine ? buildSettingGroups(engine) : []), [engine]); in SettingsPopover.tsx so the 90-row descriptor tree is rebuilt only when the engine identity changes.
findings.why_it_works: The result depends only on the engine identity, so memoising on it is safe and changes nothing observable. It removes per-frame work from the main thread, which is where the synth is also competing for time.
findings.why_it_matters: Typing a digit, holding an arrow key, or committing any slider drag in the Settings popover updates `PlayerShell`'s `settings` state or `apiValues` object, which re-renders `SettingsPopover` and re-invokes `buildSettingGroups(engine)` from scratch on every single edit -- not once per popover open. `buildSettingGroups` (settings-schema.ts:216) allocates a brand-new array of all 8 groups and all ~90 `SettingDescriptor`/`control` objects on each call, including fresh `enumOptions()` arrays for every enum-backed row, so none of the 90 row identities survive the rebuild. Because neither `SettingsPopover` nor `SettingRow` is wrapped in `React.memo` and `buildSettingGroups()` is called directly in the render body (no `useMemo`), React has to reconcile all 90 `SettingRow` elements on every keystroke -- not just the one row the person is editing. At 90 simple form rows this is unlikely to single-handedly drop a frame, but it is pure waste on a path a one-line fix removes entirely.

findings.title: Scroll-container bound is satisfied by construction; vertical containment is gone
findings.whats_wrong: The new scroll-container branch of the hit-area gate cannot fail vertically. `contentTop + height <= scrollHeight` is true by definition for any child of a scroll container, and nothing checks that the container itself is on screen - so the window-bottom check was removed for all popover content and nothing replaced it.
findings.proposed_fix: Keep the content-range test but add the container's own containment inside the `if (scrollAncestor)` branch: fail when `ar.bottom > globalThis.innerHeight + 0.5 || ar.top < -0.5 || ar.right > globalThis.innerWidth + 0.5 || ar.left < -0.5`.
findings.why_it_works: Checking the container's own rectangle restores the property the relaxation silently assumed - that the scrolling box is itself on screen. The content-range test stays for what it genuinely covers, so a row below the fold inside a visible popover still passes, which was the point of the change.
findings.why_it_matters: Inside any scrolling ancestor the gate no longer has a vertical containment check at all, so a control clipped past the top or bottom of the window passes green. The new branch claims to bound the element by its scroll container's content range, but that bound is arithmetically free: `contentTop = r.top - ar.top + scrollAncestor.scrollTop` is the element's offset inside the scrollable content measured from the container's border-box top, so for any in-flow descendant `contentTop >= 0` and `contentTop + r.height <= scrollHeight` both hold by definition — neither condition can ever fire. What actually makes a below-the-fold row reachable is that the CONTAINER is on screen, and that is never checked, while the old `r.bottom > innerHeight` / `r.top < -0.5` test is dropped (it survives only in the `else` branch at lines 116-121). The branch also triggers on any ancestor whose computed overflowY is `auto` or `scroll` without confirming it actually overflows, and Base UI's ScrollArea Viewport hard-codes `overflow: 'scroll'`, so both popovers sit in the relaxed branch permanently, overflowing or not. Adding the container's own window-edge test restores the protection while keeping the intended 'a row below the fold is one scroll away' relaxation.

With the ScrollArea Viewport carrying no border, both conditions are unsatisfiable.

Constructed scenario: give the Settings popup a taller cap (or open it in a short window where Base UI's Positioner cannot fit it) so the panel's own scroll viewport hangs past the window bottom. Rows in the off-window part of the container are not reachable by scrolling the container — the container itself is what is off-screen — yet the filter evaluates only contentTop (always in range) and the two horizontal tests, and returns green.

findings.title: Mixer and toast skips also disable the off-screen containment check
findings.whats_wrong: The two new skips in the hit-area gate run BEFORE the element's rectangle is measured, so they exempt mixer and toast controls from the off-screen position check as well as the 44px size check. Their own comments justify only the size exemption.
findings.proposed_fix: Move the two skips below `const r = el.getBoundingClientRect()` and apply them only to the size verdict: `const sizeExempt = el.closest('[data-sonner-toast], [data-slot="track-row"], [data-slot="master-row"]') !== null;`, run the window/scroll position branches for every element, and end the filter with `return sizeExempt ? false : r.width < 44 || r.height < 44;`
findings.why_it_works: Measuring first and exempting only the size verdict keeps the deliberate 34px and 20px boxes passing, which is what the comments actually argue for, while restoring the containment check for the entire Tracks popover. The mixer's fixed-width grid makes a narrow window the realistic failure, so this is the case that matters.
findings.why_it_matters: A mixer control that is pushed off the screen now passes the merge-blocking hit-area gate silently. The two new `return false` skips are justified in their own comments as SIZE exemptions (sonner's fixed 20x20 close button, the mixer's deliberate 34px boxes), but both run BEFORE `const r = el.getBoundingClientRect()` on line 81, so they also remove those controls from the position/containment test that the narrow-700px case's own comment calls out as the thing that 'lets this fail on a control pushed past the viewport edge rather than one merely painted small'. Every control in the Tracks popover is inside one of the two exempted roots, so the whole mixer is now unmeasured on both axes: the four staff toggles, the per-row expand button, the render/solo/mute toggles, the track volume rail, the two transposition rails and the whole Master footer (select-all solo, select-all mute, master volume, the track-layout switch). The fix keeps the intended 34px/20px size exemption while restoring containment, by reading the rect first, running the position checks unconditionally, and applying the exemption only to the final 44px size return.

substitutions_disclosed: Persona prompt assets were passed to each reviewer as a file PATH to read rather than inlined into the spawn prompt (~73 KB read twice avoided). Same content, same contract.
The trivial-PR pre-check was resolved inline rather than by a subagent: a 7,166-line feature PR with 48 commits is unambiguously not a dependency bump.

The Stage 5b validator batch and the code-review-loop's own VERIFY-CHECK (superpowers:receiving-code-review, From External Reviewers) were run as ONE dispatched pass, since both ask the same question of the same findings. Both contracts were bound into the verifier's prompt.
